newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-TIGERS' TRAMMELL RETIRES AFTER GETTING TWO HITS.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-TIGERS' TRAMMELL RETIRES AFTER GETTING TWO HITS.

text.p: Detroit Tigers veteran shortstop Alan Trammell collected two hits Sunday, then announced his retirement in a brief ceremony after the game.

The 38-year-old Trammell, who spent all 20 of his major-league seasons with the Tigers, singled in his last at-bat of a 10-inning 7-5 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers. After the game, he was presented second base in a 15-minute ceremony.

"I wasn't great in any one area, but I'd like to think I was good in a lot of areas," Trammell told the fans at Tiger Stadium. "I've lived a fantasy life all these years. There have been ups and downs, but that's what life is about."
Batting second and playing his familiar shortstop, Trammell singled in the third inning off Jeff D'Amico. He added a sacrifice fly in the fifth and singled in the 10th off Mike Fetters.

"I started with a base hit up the middle off Reggie Cleveland (in 1977) and I ended it with a hit up the middle," Trammell said. "It meant a ton to get that hit. It was once in my life I was selfish. I wanted to end with a hit."

Trammell received a standing ovation when he came to the plate in the first inning. He received another when he batted in the seventh with the Tigers leading 5-2. But Milwaukee rallied for three runs in the eighth, giving Trammell another at-bat.
After Trammell's final hit, the fans, teammates and Brewers players gave him his third standing ovation.

"He played the game the way he wanted to play it and it was the right way," Tigers manager Buddy Bell said. "The thing I admire about him most is his sincerity. He's a caring, sincere guy. I was hoping he'd go out with a good game and he did."

"He's in a mould of a (Robin) Yount and a (Paul) Molitor from what I've observed," Brewers manager Phil Garner said. "I wish we could run films of these guys to show the kids how the game is played, running everything out, giving 100 percent. They're special people."
Trammell has suffered through various injuries over the past several years. He played just 66 games this season due to left ankle problems and hit .233 with one home run and 16 RBI.

"I can't fight it anymore," Trammell said. "There comes a point you have to give into it. The last couple of years, I've tried to be a role player, but I couldn't do the job like I wanted to. I looked at my performance and it wasn't up to par. It was time to move on."
Trammell will remain with the team in an unspecified job.

Trammell came up in 1977 and formed the most prolific double-play combination in American League history with second baseman Lou Whitaker, appearing in 1,918 games together. He was selected to six All-Star Games, playing in four, and ranks on the team's top-10 list in nine primary categories.

Trammell enjoyed his best season in 1987 when he batted .343 with 28 homers, 105 RBI, 109 runs and 21 steals to finish second in A.L. Most Valuable Player voting. He finished his career with 185 homers, 1,003 RBI and 1,231 runs scored in 2,293 games.
